title: Multi-Resolution Wire-Fencing for Efficient Path Sampling
authors: Simen Z. Stenersen Michler, Lukas Baldauf, Titus S. van Erp
abstract: Path sampling methods enable the computation of thermodynamic and kinetic properties through Monte Carlo (MC) moves that generate trajectories from short forward and backward molecular dynamics (MD) segments. Recently, the wire-fencing move was developed to achieve near-unity acceptance while also rapidly decorrelating successive paths, two properties that are usually in conflict in conventional MC schemes. However, in large systems, such as biomolecular simulations, the frame-saving frequency is often kept low to reduce storage requirements. Likewise, when evaluating the order parameter is expensive, frames are saved less frequently to reduce the associated cost. In either situation, this can severely limit the number of available shooting points, in extreme situations leaving only a single point, typically the one with the highest order parameter value, accessible for shooting. Repeated shootings may then originate from the same configuration, reducing sampling efficiency. Here, we introduce a multi-resolution variant of the wire-fencing move in which selected subtrajectories are propagated at higher temporal resolution than the stored trajectories. This refinement affects only the MC move and does not alter the structure or storage of the generated paths, but enhances the diffusion of shooting points along the trajectory and thereby improves sampling efficiency. The approach is demonstrated on two model systems and a realistic protein--ligand unbinding process, with the latter showing an estimated efficiency improvement of more than an order of magnitude.
summary: This paper introduces the Multi-Resolution Wire-Fencing (MRWF) move to overcome sampling bottlenecks in path sampling simulations. By temporarily refining sub-trajectories at higher resolution, MRWF dramatically increases the diversity of available shooting points. This leads to substantial, often order-of-magnitude, improvements in the statistical efficiency of calculating rare-event kinetics.
main_problem: The primary challenge is efficiently sampling rare events in complex systems, such as protein unbinding, using path sampling methods.
main_result: The proposed Multi-Resolution Wire-Fencing (MRWF) move significantly improves sampling efficiency by enhancing the diversity of available shooting points along the trajectory.
method: MRWF refines the standard wire-fencing move by propagating selected sub-trajectories at a higher temporal resolution than the stored path frames.
model_or_system: The methods are tested on model systems including a 1D double-well potential, a puckering example, and a realistic protein–ligand unbinding process.
key_observables: Sampling efficiency, shooting-point diversity ($D_{shot}$), crossing-probability profiles, and estimated rate constants.
important_parameters: Frame-saving frequency (low frequency limits sampling), temporal resolution, and the order parameter ($\lambda(x)$) defining the reaction coordinate.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the underlying path sampling framework (like super-detailed balance) can be maintained while introducing higher-resolution intermediate steps.
figures_summary: Figures compare MRWF and WF performance, showing improved crossing-probability profiles and significantly reduced repetition of successive shooting points for MRWF.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the MRWF move, derives its acceptance criteria using super-detailed balance, and then validates its superior performance by comparing it against conventional wire-fencing on multiple model systems.
why_interesting: While focused on classical MD/path sampling, the core concept of enhancing sampling efficiency by refining intermediate states echoes challenges in simulating complex quantum dynamics or open quantum systems where rare transitions are key.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Schematic illustration of a wire-fencing (WF) move in the [i+] ensemble, showing how a new path is generated through a sequence of shorter subtrajectories.

FIG. 2: Illustration of a wire-fencing (WF) move in which multiple subtrajectories originate from the same shooting point. This scarcity of shooting points can arise from infrequent frame saving, corresponding to a high subcycle number, while at the same time, steep gradients on the potential energy surface lead to a rapid decrease in the order parameter during shooting. Colors, markers, and line styles have the same meaning as in Fig. 1.

FIG. 3: Illustration of the multi-resolution wire-fencing move. Colors, markers, and line styles have the same meaning as in Fig. 1, with the smaller spheres representing the high-resolution points. This example illustrates how a new path is obtained from an old path using two sets of three subtrajectories. s5 is a rejected subtrajectory, and s4 is therefore used again to select a shooting point for generating s6.

FIG. 4: Comparison of MRWF and conventional wire-fencing for the double-well, puckering, and T4L L99A/benzene systems. Panels (a,b), (c,d), and (e,f) correspond to the double-well, puckering, and T4L systems, respectively; within each pair, the first panel shows the crossing-probability profile and the second the corresponding running rate estimate as a function of Monte Carlo moves. Insets in (a) and (c) show the endpoint region of the double-well and puckering crossing-probability profiles on a linear scale. The vertical dashed lines in panels (a), (c), and (e) represent the interface positions.
